issues.legal_issue: A voluntary and reliable extra-judicial confession may provide the basis for a conviction even without independent corroboration.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness to the killing, and the prosecution relied principally on the accused’s extra-judicial confession and circumstantial evidence.

Two witnesses testified that the accused confessed immediately after the occurrence; the courts found their evidence reliable and the confession voluntary, with no inducement, threat, promise, coercion, or pressure shown.
The confession was supported by evidence of disclosures and recoveries, including the weapon and a bloodstained sheet.
issues.conclusion: The confession to the reliable witnesses was voluntary and could be relied on; considered with the other proved circumstances, it supported the conviction.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles in Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh, Maghar Singh v. State of Punjab, Narayan Singh v. State of M.P., Kishore Chand v. State of H.P., Baldev Raj v. State of Haryana, Piara Singh v. State of Punjab, and Madan Gopal Kakkad v. Naval Dubey, an extra-judicial confession is not inherently weak and may alone sustain conviction if the court finds it true, voluntary, and reliable. The court must examine its circumstances and ensure it was not induced by a threat, promise, or inducement within Section 24 of the Evidence Act or procured in suspicious circumvention of Sections 25 and 26.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and confession_extra_judicial and confession_voluntary and confession_reliable

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.confession_extra_judicial: The accused made a confession outside a formal judicial proceeding to another person.
predicates.confession_voluntary: The accused made the confession without inducement, threat, promise, coercion, or pressure.
predicates.confession_reliable: The court found the confession and the witness who recounted it credible after considering the circumstances in which it was made.

issues.definition: When a conviction is under appeal and the court finds an extra-judicial confession voluntary and reliable, the confession may itself support the conviction.

issues.legal_issue: Permission to cross-examine a party’s own witness does not automatically erase that witness’s evidence, and a credible part of the evidence may still be relied on.
material_facts: A prosecution witness supported the allegation that the accused had confessed.
The prosecutor was permitted to cross-examine that witness only concerning a discrepancy about when the first information report was lodged.
The witness’s account of the confession was not the subject of that limited cross-examination and remained credible in the courts’ assessment.
issues.conclusion: The witness’s evidence about the confession was admissible and could be relied on; the witness’s limited cross-examination did not erase that evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 142 and 154 of the Indian Evidence Act govern leading questions and a party’s ability to cross-examine its own witness; Section 155 concerns impeaching a witness’s credit. As explained in Sat Paul v. Delhi Administration, Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana, and Rabindra Kumar Dey v. State of Orissa, permission to cross-examine a witness does not wash the evidence off the record. The fact-finder may rely on a creditworthy part after considering the testimony as a whole, with due caution. Permission under Section 154 is discretionary and must be exercised judicially, not granted merely on a party’s request.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which a witness gives evidence.
predicates.witness_cross_examined_by_calling_party: The court permits the party that called a witness to question that witness in the manner of cross-examination.
predicates.testimony_part_remains_credible: After considering the testimony as a whole and the effect of the questioning, the fact-finder finds a part of the witness’s evidence credible.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, a credible part of a witness’s evidence remains usable even after the calling party has cross-examined that witness.

issues.legal_issue: A confession made after arrest to a witness who is not a police officer is inadmissible.
material_facts: One witness arrived in the village after the accused had already been arrested.
The alleged confession to that witness was said to have been made after the arrest.
issues.conclusion: The alleged confession to that witness was inadmissible and could not be relied on as evidence of the confession.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that a confession made after the accused’s arrest to a witness arriving after the arrest was inadmissible, consistent with the restriction on confessions made in custody to persons other than police officers in Section 26 of the Evidence Act.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to prove a confession.
predicates.accused_arrested_before_statement: The accused had been arrested before the alleged confession was made.
predicates.confession_made_after_arrest_to_non_poli: After arrest, the accused allegedly confessed to a witness who was not a police officer.

issues.definition: A confession allegedly made after arrest to a non-police witness cannot be admitted in a criminal trial.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to identify the origin of blood on a recovered item does not by itself deprive the recovery evidence of probative value.
material_facts: The accused made a disclosure that led to recovery of a sheet concealed in his house and of the weapon.
The sheet and other articles were found to bear human blood, but the origin of the blood could not be determined after the passage of time.
The recoveries and the related disclosure evidence were accepted by the courts.
issues.conclusion: The inability to determine the blood’s origin did not entitle the accused to an acquittal or require the recovery evidence to be rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Applying State of Rajasthan v. Teja Ram, and distinguishing the fact-specific circumstances in Prabhu Babaji Navle v. State of Bombay, Raghav Prapanna Tripathi v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Kansa Behera v. State of Orissa, the court held that failure to determine the origin of blood due to disintegration does not mean the blood was not human or automatically render a recovery valueless. The evidence must be assessed in the circumstances of the case, rather than discarded on that ground alone.

predicates.criminal_case_based_on_circumstantial_ev: The prosecution seeks to prove the offence through circumstantial evidence rather than eyewitness testimony.
predicates.item_recovered_at_accused_disclosure: The accused gave information that led to the discovery and recovery of an item.
predicates.blood_detected_on_item: Testing detected blood on the recovered item.
predicates.blood_origin_unidentified_due_to_degrada: The origin of the blood could not be determined because it had degraded or disintegrated.

issues.definition: When an item is recovered following the accused’s disclosure and blood is detected but its origin cannot be determined because of degradation, that failure alone does not nullify the recovery evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Omission to record the dimensions of bloodstains does not, by itself, require rejection of the prosecution evidence.
material_facts: The seizure documentation did not state the dimensions of the bloodstains on the sheet and other articles.
The accused did not show how that omission adversely affected the prosecution case or establish that the evidence had been fabricated to implicate him.
The recovery and related circumstances were otherwise found proved.
issues.conclusion: The omission was not fatal and did not create a reasonable doubt requiring rejection of the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Kansa Behera v. State of Orissa as a decision confined to its facts, holding that the significance of omitted stain dimensions depends on the circumstances. The omission may matter where a defence or allegation of fabrication makes it material, but the accused is entitled only to the benefit of reasonable doubt, not a speculative doubt.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution relies on bloodstained articles.
predicates.bloodstain_dimensions_not_recorded: The seizure record or other evidence does not state the dimensions of the bloodstains.
predicates.no_specific_adverse_effect_shown: The accused has not shown that the omission materially undermines the evidence or supports a claim that the evidence was fabricated.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, an omission to record bloodstain dimensions does not alone require rejection of the evidence when no specific adverse effect is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction may be sustained where the proved confession, disclosures, recoveries, and forensic circumstances collectively connect the accused to the offence beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The death was found to be homicidal, and the injuries supported the finding of murder.
Reliable witnesses testified to a voluntary confession, and the accused’s disclosure statements led to recovery of the weapon and a concealed sheet bearing human blood.
An item recovered with the weapon bore a human hair, and the hair was found on examination to be human; the other proved circumstances were also considered by the courts.
The trial court convicted the accused and the High Court affirmed the conviction.
issues.conclusion: The combined circumstances sufficiently connected the accused with the murder; the conviction was affirmed and the appeal dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the circumstantial evidence cumulatively and found the confession, disclosure-led recoveries, and forensic findings sufficient. Applying State of Rajasthan v. Teja Ram on the blood evidence and the principles governing voluntary extra-judicial confessions and credible witness testimony, it held that the evidence proved the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and homicidal_death_proved and voluntary_confession_proved and disclosure_led_recoveries_proved and forensic_circumstances_support_accused_link

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.homicidal_death_proved: The evidence establishes that the victim died through a criminal act.
predicates.voluntary_confession_proved: Reliable evidence establishes that the accused voluntarily confessed to the offence.
predicates.disclosure_led_recoveries_proved: The accused’s information led to proved recovery of items connected with the offence.
predicates.forensic_circumstances_support_accused_l: Forensic findings concerning recovered items provide support for connecting the accused to the offence.

issues.definition: A conviction is sustainable when, in an appeal, homicidal death, a voluntary confession, disclosure-led recoveries, and supporting forensic circumstances are proved together.
